Learn step by step

Read the simple explanation first, then open the source-based detail.

1. Invention vs Innovation vs Improvement

Easy way to remember: invention = create something new; innovation = use an idea to create value; improvement = make something existing better.

TermMeaning in the PDFPDF example
InventionCreating something entirely new that did not exist before.Invention of the lightbulb.
InnovationApplying a novel idea in a useful way to create value.Smartphones combining camera, phone and internet.
ImprovementEnhancing an existing product or process.Upgrading a laptop to make it faster.

2. Types of innovation — technology/market novelty matrix

The PDF gives four types: incremental, disruptive, architectural and radical innovation.

Incremental

Small improvements or upgrades to existing products/services.

Example: new smartphone versions with better cameras.

Disruptive

A product/service disrupts existing markets.

Example: Netflix disrupting traditional cable TV.

Architectural

Reconfigures existing systems in a new way.

Example: smart homes integrating sensors and mobile apps.

Radical

Creates completely new industries, as described in the notes.

Example: invention of the internet.
The PDF’s page 2 matrix compares existing/new markets with existing/new technologies. The source diagram is available in the PDF Diagrams tab.

3. Types by area of application

  • Product innovation: new or significantly improved goods/services. PDF example: electric vehicles such as Tesla introducing new features.
  • Process innovation: new or significantly improved production/delivery methods. Example: Amazon warehouse robotics.
  • Marketing innovation: changes in design, packaging, placement, promotion or pricing. Example: Coca-Cola personalized name bottles.
  • Organizational innovation: new methods in business practices, workplace organization or external relations. Example: Google’s 20% time policy.

4. Why innovation matters

According to the PDF, innovation supports economic growth, quality of life and responses to challenges such as climate change, food scarcity and healthcare.

  • Competitive advantage — stay ahead of the market.
  • Customer satisfaction — deliver new value and experiences.
  • Efficiency — optimize processes and reduce waste.
  • Impact — address societal and environmental issues.

5. Creativity techniques

Brainstorming

A group technique for generating many ideas to solve a problem. Rules: defer judgment, encourage wild ideas, go for quantity, and build on others’ ideas.

PDF example: fitness app ideas such as heart-rate tracking, sleep monitoring, GPS tracking and AI coaching.

Mind mapping

A visual technique: put the central idea in the middle and branch out into related subtopics. It structures thoughts, supports nonlinear thinking and reveals connections.

PDF example: a smart fridge mind map with sensors, mobile app, energy efficiency and inventory management.

SCAMPER

A checklist to generate ideas by modifying an existing product or service:

  1. S — Substitute: what can be changed?
  2. C — Combine: what can be combined?
  3. A — Adapt: what can be borrowed/adapted?
  4. M — Modify: what can change in appearance or function?
  5. P — Put to another use: can it serve another purpose?
  6. E — Eliminate: what can be removed?
  7. R — Reverse/Rearrange: can the order or roles be changed?

PDF example: improve a backpack with solar panels, a built-in charger or a foldable design.

6. Innovation lifecycle — 7 stages

  1. Idea Generation — source ideas through brainstorming, feedback or observation.
  2. Idea Screening — evaluate and filter ideas with potential.
  3. Concept Development — refine and design the concept.
  4. Prototype Creation — build a preliminary model.
  5. Testing and Validation — test in real-world conditions.
  6. Commercialization — launch the product/service.
  7. Scaling and Improvement — expand and refine using user input.

PDF example: smart water bottle idea → screening → prototype with hydration reminders → athlete testing → launch and scaling.

7. Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs)

TRLs assess technology maturity and how close it is to deployment. The PDF describes nine levels:

  1. Basic principles observed and reported.
  2. Technology concept/application formulated.
  3. Analytical and experimental proof of concept.
  4. Component validation in a laboratory environment.
  5. Component validation in a relevant environment.
  6. System/subsystem model or prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment.
  7. System prototype demonstrated in an operational environment.
  8. Actual system completed and qualified through testing and demonstration.
  9. Actual system proven through successful mission operations.

PDF example: a drone delivery system may start at TRL 2 during concept discussions and reach TRL 9 after successful commercial operation.

8. Structure of an effective idea pitch

  1. Problem statement: clearly define the issue.
  2. Solution: present the idea/product/service.
  3. Target audience: identify who benefits.
  4. Benefits: explain advantages over alternatives.
  5. Feasibility: show it can realistically be implemented.

PDF example: food-waste app that notifies local NGOs when surplus food is available. Target: colleges and food-rescue NGOs. Benefits: reduces waste and feeds people. Feasibility: GPS and inventory tracking.

9. Case studies and activities in the PDF

  • Swiggy early pitch: problem of limited time to cook/dine; solution connecting users, restaurants and delivery partners; enabled by GPS, mobile payments and restaurant partnerships.
  • Airbnb: started with renting air mattresses during a conference; developed a website, tested listing/booking functions and scaled.
  • Telephone: communication need → experiments/prototype → validation → commercial product.
  • Tesla TRL progression: PDF maps battery research through prototypes/testing to mass production.
  • Unit activities: Innovation Hunt, SCAMPER Workshop and a 3-minute idea pitch.

Exam writing practice

2-mark and 4-mark answers

Use these as study structures. Confirm your exact exam pattern with your teacher; the PDF itself does not specify marks.

2 marks: Define innovation.

Innovation is the process of translating creative ideas into tangible and valuable products, services or processes. It creates practical benefits and supports growth and progress.

2 marks: What is brainstorming?

Brainstorming is a group creativity technique used to generate a large number of ideas to solve a problem. Its rules include deferring judgment, encouraging unusual ideas, aiming for quantity and building on others’ ideas.

2 marks: What are TRLs?

Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) are a framework used to assess the maturity of a technology and how close it is to deployment. The PDF lists nine levels, from basic principles observed (TRL 1) to successful mission operations (TRL 9).

4 marks: Differentiate invention, innovation and improvement.

InventionInnovationImprovement
Creates something entirely new.Applies a novel idea usefully to create value.Enhances an existing product or process.
Lightbulb (PDF example)Smartphone combining camera, phone and internetUpgrading a laptop to make it faster

4 marks: Explain SCAMPER.

SCAMPER is a checklist for modifying an existing product or service to generate ideas:

  1. Substitute — change a component.
  2. Combine — join features or products.
  3. Adapt — borrow a useful feature from elsewhere.
  4. Modify — change appearance or function.
  5. Put to another use — use for a different purpose.
  6. Eliminate — remove unnecessary parts.
  7. Reverse/Rearrange — reverse roles or change order.

Example from the PDF: a backpack can be redesigned with solar panels, a built-in charger or a foldable design.

4 marks: Write the seven stages of the innovation lifecycle.

  1. Idea Generation
  2. Idea Screening
  3. Concept Development
  4. Prototype Creation
  5. Testing and Validation
  6. Commercialization
  7. Scaling and Improvement

Example from the PDF: a smart water bottle is conceived, screened, prototyped with reminders, tested among athletes, launched and scaled.

4 marks: Explain the structure of an idea pitch.

  1. Problem Statement — define the issue.
  2. Solution — explain the idea.
  3. Target Audience — state who benefits.
  4. Benefits — show the value.
  5. Feasibility — show realistic implementation.

PDF example: an app connects college canteens with NGOs to collect surplus food, reducing waste and helping people in need.
